extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators and patent prosecutors (patent practitioners advising on or drafting claims under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f))
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when §112(f) (means/step‑plus‑function) is triggered, what corresponding structure/material/acts (SMA) must be disclosed, prosecution tactics, and how litigants should invoke or defend §112(f) in drafting, prosecution, and litigation (including life‑sciences and method claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: 112(f) Trigger Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of “means”: presumption against 112(f) applying. Test: does the element recite a function without particular structure, material, or acts (SMA) sufficient to perform the function?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: an absence of the word “means” creates a presumption that §112(f) does not apply, but the dispositive inquiry is whether the claim element merely recites a function without reciting sufficient SMA to perform it. This is a question of law (claim construction). Examples in the slides ask: 'Does any part of this claim trigger construction under Sec. 112(f)? Why? Why not?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding Structure/Material/Acts (SMA) Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: "… described in the specification …." (requirements for corresponding SMA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated guidance from the slides: (1) Corresponding SMA must be described in the specification; (2) Saying the function is performed in a known or conventional way is insufficient; (3) The specification or prosecution history must clearly link the corresponding SMA to the claim‑recited function; (4) Corresponding SMA is limited to that necessary to perform the function; (5) SMA recited in a dependent claim can be included; (6) A generic computer or processor without an algorithm is normally insufficient SMA; (7) Determination is a question of law (claim construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of Inadequate SMA Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification fails to disclose corresponding SMA necessary to perform a claimed function, the claim can be invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete consequence: inadequate SMA disclosure can invalidate the claim under 35 U.S.C. §112(b) (indefiniteness / lack of particular and distinct claiming). The slides present this as a direct outcome of failing to identify adequate corresponding SMA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement under §112(f): Literal and Equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Literal infringement requires the accused device/practice to perform the same function in substantially the same way to achieve the same result; equivalents require substantially the same function, way, and result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional guidance: In evaluating 'substantially the same way', give greater weight to components in the identified SMA that play a central role in performing the function. If the accused equivalent arose before the patent filing, the doctrine of equivalents analysis for an equivalent SMA may collapse into the literal equivalence analysis. See slides on literal vs equivalents and relationship to timing of accused equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply §112(f) to Method Claims — underlying function vs acts
rubrics_metrics.description: If a method claim element recites only the underlying function without acts explaining how to accomplish it, §112(f) (step‑plus‑function) applies even absent express ‘step for’ language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seal‑Flex (Rader, J.) guidance: the 'underlying function' corresponds to what the element accomplishes; 'acts' correspond to how it is accomplished. If only the function is recited, §112(f) governs. The slides note non‑precedential Fed. Cir. decisions (Dionex, Intelligent Automation) showing method steps can trigger §112(f). A practical objection is difficulty identifying corresponding 'acts' in the spec; response: routinely treat algorithms as 'structure' and cite them as corresponding SMA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying §112(f) in Life Sciences Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Life‑sciences/functionally‑worded claims can and have been treated under §112(f); drafters should not limit corresponding disclosure to 'structure' alone and should include 'acts' (or other non‑structure disclosures) that show how the function is performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ex parte Gleave — the Board limited disclosure to specific antisense oligonucleotides and RNAi molecules and equivalents; recommended drafting techniques include describing 'acts' by which an antibody binds or blocks (e.g., 'one way the isolated monoclonal antibody binds ... is by doing the following acts: ...'). Also propose drafting claims that combine functional recitation with structure (variable and constant domains) or 'complementary determining means' to help tie function to structure/acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: §112(f) as a Shield Against Alice/Mayo Eligibility Attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking §112(f) can incorporate specification details into claim scope, satisfying the 'how' requirement and thereby help defend against subject‑matter eligibility (Alice/Mayo) attacks that target purely result‑oriented claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: courts have required claims to identify 'how' a functional result is achieved; §112(f) incorporates corresponding SMA from the specification into the claim, which can ground the 'how'. The slides cite American Axle, IBM (Zillow), Hawk Tech, and Internet Patents as examples of courts faulting claims for being result‑oriented without explaining how to accomplish tasks; the presenter argues §112(f) can be used to avoid that problem. Note: parties and courts have not uniformly used §112(f) this way, but Fed. Cir. has 'hinted' at the shield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine Ambiguity Over Whether §112(f) Is Triggered May Violate §112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine ambiguity about whether §112(f) applies can make a claim indefinite under §112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators/examples of genuine ambiguity include conflicting intrinsic evidence on: (a) whether the claim is to a 'combination'; (b) whether the claim recites structure/material/acts sufficient to perform the function; (c) whether the claim recites a 'means' or 'step for' performing a specified function; (d) whether the applicant or examiner treated the element as a §112(f) element. The slides cite MPEP 2181 II.A. and argue that such ambiguity can be a §112(b) violation. Also: all claim construction is a question of law, and the drafter could have made triggering clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution 'How' Inventory (Checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prosecution checklist for each claim‑recited function/result: identify how it is performed/achieved in the application; whether 'how' is recited in the claim; and whether 'how' is clearly linked to the function in the specification or prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matrix from slides: columns include 'Claim‑recited function or result', 'How performed or achieved in appln.?', 'How recited in claim?', 'How clearly linked to the function, in Spec. or PH?'. Use this during drafting and prosecution to ensure corresponding SMA is present and linked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by Reference Constraints for SMA
rubrics_metrics.description: Corresponding structure necessary for a means‑plus‑function clause may not be incorporated by reference from non‑patent publications; incorporation from a U.S. patent or published U.S. patent application may be permissible but law is unsettled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law: Default Proof (Fed. Cir. 2005), Atmel (Fed. Cir. 1999) suggest material necessary to satisfy indefiniteness cannot be incorporated from non‑patent publications; Otto Bock suggested corresponding structure may be incorporated from a U.S. patent or published U.S. application but not from a non‑patent publication. 37 C.F.R. §1.57(d) treats essential material support and limits what may be incorporated. Practical prosecution tip: be cautious relying on incorporation by reference to supply required SMA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution: Expressly Associate 'Acts' with Method Steps and Functions in the Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting the specification, explicitly describe one or more ways (acts) of performing a claimed function so those acts can be relied on as corresponding SMA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample drafting phrasing from slides: 'One way to adhere the mat to the foundation ... is to spread an adhesive tack coating. Another way ... is to do the following acts: ...' or 'One way the isolated monoclonal antibody binds ... is by doing the following acts: ...'. Use such explicit 'one way' language to tie acts to claimed functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution: Associate SMA with Functional Life Sciences Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: For functional life‑sciences claims, include specification paragraphs that expressly describe 'structures, materials and acts by which' the disclosed molecule/antibody performs the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested spec language: 'The following paragraphs describe embodiments of structures, materials and acts by which the disclosed antibody binds to at least two of the following residues ...' Use explicit embodiments and examples (e.g., specific sequences, examples, algorithms) to supply corresponding SMA and equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits and Strategic Uses of §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical benefits for patent owners and challengers in asserting or contesting §112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits for patent owners: avoid invalidity for pure functional claiming (under §101, §112(a), or §112(b)), avoid invalidity over prior art while sometimes preserving an infringement fact question. Benefits for challengers/defendants: obtain narrowed constructions for non‑infringement and win §112(b) invalidity when the specification lacks support or when there is a genuine ambiguity over whether §112(f) triggered. Slides list these as strategic tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic Computer/Processor Without Algorithm Is Normally Insufficient SMA
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic computer or processor recitation, standing alone and without an algorithm or instruction of how it performs the function, is normally insufficient to satisfy the SMA requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: when drafting computer‑implemented claims, include algorithmic detail, flowcharts, or specific acts/structure in the spec so that a computer recitation can be tied to corresponding SMA and not be treated as purely functional.
